subject: chemistry
title: Mass spectrometry of organic compounds
key_idea: A mass spectrometer ionises molecules and sorts the ions by m/z. The highest peak gives the relative molecular mass, the fragments show parts of the structure, and a precise mass gives the molecular formula.

blocks.text: A mass spectrometer ionises molecules and sorts the ions by mass-to-charge ratio, m/z. This section covers how the spectrum gives the relative molecular mass.

items.meaning: The molecule with one electron removed. It keeps the whole molecule's mass.
Mass-to-charge ratio. For ions with a single positive charge, m/z equals the relative mass of the ion.
A smaller positive ion formed when the molecular ion breaks up.

blocks.label: Forming the molecular ion
where: M⁺•: the molecular ion, a radical cation

items: The peak with the highest m/z is normally the molecular ion.
Its m/z value is the **relative molecular mass** of the compound.
There is often a very small peak one unit higher. It is the [M+1]⁺ peak, from molecules containing carbon-13 (about 1.1% of carbon atoms).
The molecular ion peak is the one with the highest m/z (ignoring the tiny M+1 peak).
Its m/z value equals the relative molecular mass.

blocks.text: The molecular ion is unstable. Some break into a positive fragment and an uncharged radical. This section covers reading the fragments.

items: Only the **positive** fragment is detected. The radical is not charged, so it never reaches the detector.
The peak at the highest abundance is the base peak. It is the most stable fragment, not always M⁺.
The difference between M⁺ and a fragment peak is the mass of the piece lost.
The bonds that break most easily give stable positive ions, such as those next to a C=O group.

blocks.label: Fragmentation
where: X⁺: fragment ion seen in the spectrum

diagram.alt: Pick a peak in a mass spectrum and see which ion is likely and what was lost.
diagram.prompt: Pick a fragment peak from a molecule with M⁺ at m/z 58

options.label: m/z 57
results: C₃H₅O⁺, formed by losing one hydrogen atom
1, an H atom. C₄H₉⁺ is not possible for a three-carbon molecule.

blocks.text: Matching fragment peaks to known ions lets you assemble a structure. A peak at 43 with an M⁺ of 58 suggests CH₃CO, so propanone is likely.

items: Subtract a fragment from M⁺ to find what was lost.
Learn the common fragment ions in the table.
Use the fragments to build up a structure piece by piece.

blocks.text: High-resolution mass spectrometry measures m/z to four decimal places. This section covers how a precise mass identifies a molecular formula.

items: Atoms do not have exact whole-number masses (except carbon-12, which is exactly 12).
Different formulae with the same whole-number mass have slightly different **precise masses**.
Add up the precise atomic masses for each candidate formula. The match to the measured value gives the formula.

blocks.text: A measured value of 58.0419 therefore fits C₃H₆O. The other candidates are too far away.

items: Whole-number masses cannot tell apart formulae of the same nominal mass.
Four decimal places can: sum the precise masses and compare.

checks.q: The mass spectrum of an alcohol has its highest m/z peak at 60 and a large peak at 31. Suggest what the peak at 31 shows.
checks.a: M⁺ at 60 shows the relative molecular mass is 60. The peak at 31 is CH₂OH⁺, so the alcohol is a primary alcohol such as propan-1-ol.

checks.q: Explain why only some fragments appear as peaks in a mass spectrum.
checks.a: Only positively charged fragments are accelerated and detected. Radicals and neutral molecules have no charge, so they are not detected.

checks.q: A compound has a precise mass of 44.0261. Decide whether it is C₂H₄O (precise masses H 1.0078, C 12.0000, O 15.9949) and show your working.
checks.a: C₂H₄O = 24.0000 + 4.0312 + 15.9949 = 44.0261, which matches 44.0261 to four decimal places, so it is C₂H₄O.

blocks.text: Counting carbon atoms from the M+1 peak
About 1.1% of carbon atoms are carbon-13, so the [M+1]⁺ peak grows with the number of carbons in the molecule.

blocks.label: Number of carbon atoms
blocks.formula: n = 100 × abundance of [M+1]⁺ ÷ (1.1 × abundance of M⁺)
where: n: number of carbon atoms in the molecule

blocks.text: An [M+1]⁺ of 3.3 and an M⁺ of 50 give n = 100 × 3.3 ÷ (1.1 × 50) = 6, so the compound has six carbon atoms.
Finding bromine or chlorine from the M+2 peak

items: Chlorine has two isotopes, ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl, in the ratio about 3 : 1. A chlorine compound has an [M+2]⁺ peak about one third the height of M⁺.
Bromine has two isotopes, ⁷⁹Br and ⁸¹Br, in the ratio about 1 : 1. A bromine compound has an [M+2]⁺ peak about the same height as M⁺.
Without an M+2 peak of this size, the compound has no chlorine or bromine.
